sections.title: Answer the AI question
sections.intro: "How do you use AI in your day-to-day work?" The usual mistake here is answering too analytically, with a tour of tools and features, when the interviewer is listening for judgment. Build a better answer one step at a time.

questions.prompt: What is this question really evaluating?
options: Your judgment — what you delegate, why, how you check it
Your speed — how much faster AI makes you
Your tool knowledge — which models and IDEs you use
Your enthusiasm — how much you use AI overall
questions.explanation: A tour of tools and features answers a question nobody asked. The five areas (Work, Trust, Iteration, Growth, Scaling) are all about how you think and what you own.

options: "I've tried most of the major models."
A one-day prototype that unlocked a go/no-go decision
"I use AI for basically everything now."
"I use Copilot for autocomplete all the time."
questions.explanation: The best Work answers show AI changing what was *possible*, not just shaving time off a task you already knew how to do. "Everything" reads as naive.

questions.prompt: To show judgment, what else belongs in the answer?
options: A claim that AI never makes mistakes for you
Your opinion of which vendor is best
A list of the AI tools you've rejected
A specific moment you turned AI off, and why
questions.explanation: For example: "It was producing plausible guesses without real context on our cluster, so I finished it by hand." Knowing where AI doesn't fit is as strong a signal as knowing where it does.

questions.prompt: Trust is the one area that doesn't carry over from general experience. Why?
options: Interviewers rarely ask about it
It's a new name for code review, nothing more
You only learn it by catching real AI mistakes yourself
It only applies to security teams
questions.explanation: General debugging skill carries over to an unfamiliar debugger. AI-specific verification habits don't come from anywhere else; you have to have built them in practice.

questions.prompt: Which Trust detail is most convincing?
options: "I only use the most accurate models."
"I trust it for most things at this point."
"It reused a deprecated internal API; tests caught it."
"I always double-check the output."
questions.explanation: It names a real, codebase-specific mistake and the check that caught it. "I double-check" is something everyone says, and nobody can tell whether it's true.

questions.prompt: They follow up: "What won't you paste into an AI tool?" Best answer?
options: "I don't really think about it much."
"Everything is fine if it's internal."
A line you've actually drawn: secrets, customer data, keys
"Nothing — the vendors handle security."
questions.explanation: Managing what you share is part of Trust. A clear, explicit line, ideally with how you enforce it, shows real judgment. Making it up case by case doesn't.

questions.prompt: Then a values question: "How do you think about AI adoption on a team?" What shape should the answer take?
options: A clear principle, then a concrete example
A story only, with no stated principle
A long list of pros and cons
A prediction about where AI is headed
questions.explanation: Values questions need a point of view, grounded in something real. For example: delegate what's quick to verify, stay hands-on where mistakes are costly, and look at whole workflows rather than single tasks.

sections.title: Spot the problem
sections.intro: Which AI area does it show, or what's wrong with it?

questions.prompt: "I keep a project instruction file that's grown over months — each repeat mistake becomes a rule." Which area?
options: Work — shipping a concrete outcome
Scaling — spreading practice across the org
Iteration — treating AI tooling as maintained infrastructure
Trust — verifying output correctness
questions.explanation: Iteration asks whether your approach has meaningfully changed recently based on what you've seen work or fail. A file that keeps growing is direct evidence.

questions.prompt: "I ran pairing sessions for skeptical teammates and we wrote team conventions for what goes to AI." Which area?
options: Scaling — moving good practice beyond yourself
Work — what you personally shipped
Iteration — refining your own prompts
Growth — how you personally stay current
questions.explanation: Scaling maps to Leadership. It's the area that matters most for senior roles, especially when it changes how a team works, not just how fast one person works.

questions.prompt: "I follow a lot of AI newsletters." What's missing for a strong Growth answer?
options: Nothing — reading is enough
Evidence of acting on it — what you tried after
A certification in prompt engineering
More newsletters — breadth shows commitment
questions.explanation: What makes a Growth answer strong is specifics: a named source, plus something you actually tried because of it. Just consuming content isn't the signal.

questions.prompt: Why is AI output easier to trust for code than for prose?
options: Code can be checked independently, by tests and CI
Code from AI never has bugs
Models are trained mostly on code
Prose is always lower stakes
questions.explanation: Correctness for prose is fuzzy, while code can be tested. That's why strong answers lean on testing discipline as the way to check AI-generated code.

questions.prompt: A candidate answers only with "I ship 3x faster with AI." How does that read?
options: Strong — velocity is what companies want
Fine, if they give the exact multiplier
Too modest — they should claim more
Naive — speed with no verification story
questions.explanation: On any non-trivial codebase, output is rarely right the first time. Speed with no mention of how you check the results is a Trust red flag.

questions.prompt: Why revisit your prepared AI answers regularly?
options: Interviewers memorize common answers
Companies change their AI policies yearly
The space moves fast — last quarter's answer goes stale
You shouldn't — consistency matters more
questions.explanation: A story about a workflow you've since outgrown undercuts the Iteration signal. Keep your examples recent.
